mentions.excerpt: Michael Burry, citing Apollo’s Torsten Slok, says private non-residential construction excluding data centers fell 7.9% year over year in June.
Torsten Slok, Apollo’s chief economist, turns the revenue question into an accounting test.
Torsten Slok’s earlier question was who would write the checks if technology companies’ cash flow doubled while their customers’ did not.

Torsten Slok’s fear that agents will move deposits from accounts earning the 0.1% national average to accounts yielding 3.3% to 5% is economically coherent, but Walker notes that cash-sorting fears have recurred at events including the SVB collapse and mostly failed to play out.
Torsten Slok of Apollo says adding technology analysts’ forecasts roughly doubles the sector’s operating cash flow to about $2.4 trillion by 2028, a gain of more than $1.2 trillion.
Torsten Slok and Burry tie the rate rise directly to the buildout.
Torsten Slok of Apollo reported on September 21 the consensus that the hyperscalers' operating cash flow more than triples by 2030, outrunning their capital spending.
Torsten Slok of Apollo put the gap at about four months on July 16, citing the Epoch Capabilities Index.

sides.claim: The tech silo is betting on a future in which demand for AI and tech services explodes, while the silos covering the companies that would pay for those services see a much more modest outlook, and both cannot be right at the same time.
In S&P 500 Q2 earnings season data, AI adoption keeps broadening: 69% of companies now point to a live deployment, up from 64% last quarter.

sides.question: whose-margin-pays
sides.claim: Either tech's customers will generate a lot more cash than their analysts expect, or tech's cash flow forecasts are too optimistic, which raises the question of who exactly will be writing all those checks to buy AI services.

sides.question: whose-margin-pays
sides.claim: Agentic AI assistants like Muse could soon automatically sweep household cash into accounts paying 3.3% to 5.0%, instead of leaving it in checking accounts earning the 0.1% national average.

sides.question: who-writes-the-checks
sides.claim: Rates are rising for reasons beyond a strong economy: sticky inflation is lifting yields in the front end, record hyperscaler debt issuance is pressuring the belly, and fiscal worries are pushing up the long end.

sides.question: who-writes-the-checks
sides.claim: This disclosure pattern still leaves investors without a verifiable link between AI capex and the top line.

sides.question: what-does-5-percent-do
sides.claim: Because data centers, power generation, transmission and government deficits are all long-duration claims on savings, the competition for capital concentrates at the long end of the curve, which is why long rates have moved more than short rates.

Consensus expects hyperscalers' operating cash flow to more than triple by 2030, outpacing the sharp increase in AI-driven capex, based on FactSet and Apollo Chief Economist sources for Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft and Oracle.
